jobs.title: Graduate Sustainability Consultant (2027)
jobs.summary: An entry-level consulting role in Arup's Americas Sustainability Consulting team, doing energy, carbon, comfort, water and resilience analysis that shapes buildings from single measures to master plans. Strong candidates pair a built-environment master's with hands-on simulation and whole-life carbon skills, rating-system fluency (LEED/WELL), and the ability to explain results clearly to clients and design teams.

skills.asks: Run building energy and performance optimization studies using simulation tools such as EnergyPlus, OpenStudio and IES VE.
learn: Read an EnergyPlus/OpenStudio model: zones, constructions, schedules, internal loads, HVAC systems
Pick and read a weather file (EPW) and explain how San Francisco's mild marine climate drives loads
Build a simple shoebox model and run a parametric sweep (insulation, glazing, WWR, setpoints)
Interpret outputs: end-use breakdown, EUI, peak loads, unmet hours
Understand baseline vs proposed modeling logic (ASHRAE 90.1 Appendix G concept) used for LEED energy credits
Sanity-check results against benchmarks such as ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager medians or CBECS

skills.project: Model a typical 3-story San Francisco office shoebox in OpenStudio, run 8-10 efficiency measures, and present an EUI waterfall chart showing which measures matter most in this climate.

skills.asks: Use Rhino + Grasshopper (and SketchUp) for parametric environmental analysis and visuals.
learn: Grasshopper basics: data trees, sliders, lists, and parametric geometry
Ladybug: import EPW, sun path, radiation analysis, wind rose, psychrometric chart
Honeybee: turn massing into thermal zones and daylight grids, run Radiance and EnergyPlus
Use Colibri or similar design-space exploration to batch options and plot tradeoffs
Produce clean diagrams that a non-technical architect or client can read in seconds

skills.project: Take one SF classroom or office floor plate, run sDA/ASE with Honeybee for the existing facade and two shading options, and recommend one with a short annotated graphic.

skills.asks: Knowledge of building systems including HVAC and sizing mechanical plant; efficiency and electrification strategies for building MEP.
learn: Core system types: VAV, DOAS + radiant or fan coils, VRF, air-to-water heat pumps
Heat pump fundamentals: COP, capacity drop at low temperature, refrigerant considerations
Heat recovery (ERV/HRV) and economizers, and why they matter in a mild climate
Load calcs: design days, peak heating/cooling load, rule-of-thumb checks (sf/ton)
Electrification of gas end uses: space heat, domestic hot water, cooking; electrical service implications
Read an MEP schedule and a single-line HVAC diagram

credentials.name: LEED Green Associate
credentials.why: Entry-level USGBC/GBCI credential showing baseline green building and LEED knowledge; a strong, achievable signal for a graduate role.
steps: Create a USGBC account and review the candidate handbook for current eligibility and fees
Study the LEED core concepts and credit categories using USGBC education or a reputable study guide
Take practice exams until you score consistently well
Schedule and pass the exam at a test center or via approved online proctoring
Maintain it with continuing education hours each reporting period

credentials.name: LEED AP BD+C
credentials.why: The posting prefers a LEED AP; BD+C (Building Design + Construction) is the specialty most relevant to new-build consulting work.
steps: Check current GBCI requirements (Green Associate first or a combined exam option)
Study the BD+C reference guide focusing on energy, water, materials and IEQ credits
Connect credits to analysis you already do (energy model, daylight, LCA, water balance)
Pass the specialty exam and log continuing education to maintain it

credentials.name: WELL AP

Use IWBI's official study materials and candidate guidance
Register for and pass the WELL AP exam
Maintain via continuing education as required by IWBI

tips: Mirror the posting's language: name EnergyPlus/OpenStudio, Ladybug/Honeybee, EC3/Athena/One Click LCA, and LEED where you genuinely used them
Lead each project bullet with a quantified result (e.g. 'identified measures cutting modeled EUI 28%')
Add a 1-page portfolio link with 3-4 projects from the skills map, ideally on Bay Area buildings
List coursework explicitly: building science, energy, embodied carbon, resilience, LCC, DERs
Note LEED Green Associate (or 'exam scheduled') and your availability for a 2027 start
Keep it to 1 page (2 max for a master's student) and export as a clean PDF
Expect numerical, verbal and/or logical reasoning style tests; practice timed sets beforehand
Brush up on percentages, ratios, unit conversions and reading charts/tables quickly
Take tests in a quiet place with stable internet, calculator and scratch paper if allowed
For situational or personality components, answer honestly and consistently rather than guessing the 'ideal'
Do not over-spend time on one question; accuracy and pace both count
Make sure your LinkedIn matches your resume and links to your portfolio
If you know Arup staff through events or alumni, a polite note of interest can help
Keep building portfolio projects while you wait so you have fresh material to discuss
Expect a building or site problem: e.g. a decarbonization strategy, a retrofit prioritization, or interpreting data
Structure: clarify goals and constraints, state assumptions, analyze, recommend, and name next steps
Do rough numbers out loud (EUI, payback, carbon) and sanity-check units
Consider tradeoffs across cost, carbon, comfort, resilience and equity - Arup values holistic thinking
Communicate visually: a simple chart or sketch beats dense text
Leave time for a crisp 1-minute summary of your recommendation
Prepare 6-8 STAR stories mapped to Changemakers, Innovative minds, Growth seekers and Adaptable adventurers
Be ready to walk through one portfolio project in technical depth: inputs, assumptions, limitations
Know Arup's story: founded by Ove Arup, employee trust ownership, Total Design, SDG alignment
Research recent Arup Americas sustainability or SF projects and reference one thoughtfully
Ask good questions: how graduates are mentored, mix of project scales, tools teams use
Confirm start date, base salary within the posted range, profit share and benefits
Ask about support for LEED/WELL credential costs and professional development
Clarify relocation, hybrid working expectations, and graduate development programs
Respond professionally and on time; negotiate respectfully if you have competing offers

questions.q: Tell me about a time you pushed a team or project toward a more sustainable outcome.
questions.hint: Changemakers. Show initiative, the evidence you used to persuade, and the measurable result. Acknowledge resistance and how you handled it.

questions.q: Describe a problem you solved with a new tool or method you had not used before.
questions.hint: Innovative minds. Explain why the standard approach fell short, how you learned the new tool quickly, and how you validated results.

questions.q: Tell me about feedback that changed how you work.
questions.hint: Growth seekers. Be specific about the feedback, what you changed, and evidence of improvement afterward.

questions.q: Describe a time project requirements changed late. What did you do?
questions.hint: Adaptable adventurers. Show calm reprioritization, communication with stakeholders, and delivering anyway.

questions.q: How do you manage several deadlines across different projects?
questions.hint: Cover a concrete system (tracker, time-blocking), early flagging of conflicts to leads, and a real example of juggling deliverables.

questions.q: Tell me about explaining a technical result to a non-technical audience.
questions.hint: Show audience awareness, simplifying with analogies or a single clear chart, and how you checked understanding.

questions.q: Walk me through how you would set up an energy model for a new office building.
questions.hint: Geometry and zoning, weather file, constructions, internal loads and schedules, HVAC system, then calibration or sanity checks of EUI and unmet hours. Mention baseline vs proposed if for LEED.

questions.q: What is the difference between operational and embodied carbon, and which matters more?
questions.hint: Define both with EN 15978 stages. Explain that as grids decarbonize and buildings get efficient, embodied carbon becomes a larger share, and that upfront carbon is emitted now. Answer 'it depends on the project' with reasoning.

questions.q: How would you reduce the embodied carbon of a mid-rise building's structure?
questions.hint: Build less and reuse first, optimize structural efficiency, lower-carbon concrete mixes (SCMs), recycled steel, mass timber where appropriate, and use EPDs/EC3 to specify limits.

questions.q: A client wants to electrify an existing gas-heated building. What do you look at first?
questions.hint: Loads and envelope, existing distribution (hydronic temps, ducts), heat pump options, DHW, electrical service capacity, costs and incentives, and phasing with equipment end-of-life.

questions.q: How do you evaluate whether a daylighting design is good?
questions.hint: Annual metrics like sDA and ASE, glare checks for critical views, balance with solar gain and thermal comfort, and coordination with lighting controls to actually save energy.

questions.q: How would you decide between two efficiency measures with different costs and savings?
questions.hint: Lifecycle cost with NPV and discount rate, not only simple payback; include maintenance, replacement, carbon value and non-energy benefits; run sensitivity on uncertain inputs.

questions.q: What does a grid-interactive efficient building do, and why does it matter in California?
questions.hint: Efficiency plus demand flexibility (shed, shift, modulate, generate) using storage, controls and thermal mass; California's solar-heavy grid makes evening peaks and time-varying emissions important.

questions.q: Which LEED credit categories does a sustainability consultant's analysis typically support?
questions.hint: Energy and Atmosphere (energy modeling), Water Efficiency (water calcs), Materials and Resources (LCA/EPDs), Indoor Environmental Quality (daylight, comfort). Show you know analysis feeds documentation.

questions.q: Why Arup rather than an architecture firm or another engineering consultancy?
questions.hint: Multidisciplinary Total Design, employee trust ownership and long-term thinking, scale from buildings to infrastructure, and a specific project or research piece that resonates with you.

questions.q: Which of the UN Sustainable Development Goals matters most to you in your work, and how?
questions.hint: Pick one or two (e.g. SDG 7, 11 or 13), link to concrete built-environment actions, and to Arup's stated SDG alignment.

questions.q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
questions.hint: Growing technical depth (e.g. energy and carbon specialist), credentials, leading parts of projects, and contributing to Arup's research or skills networks - realistic and tied to the role.

questions.q: Tell us about a recent sustainability policy or trend that will shape our work in the Bay Area.
questions.hint: E.g. all-electric building requirements, building performance standards, embodied carbon policy, or resilience planning for sea level rise; explain implications for clients.

cards.q: How are U-value and R-value related?
cards.a: U-value is the reciprocal of total R-value (U = 1/R).
cards.explain: U measures heat flow rate; R measures resistance. Lower U and higher R mean better insulation.
wrong: They are the same quantity in different units
U-value only applies to glazing, R-value to walls

cards.q: What is a thermal bridge?
cards.a: A path of higher conductivity that lets heat bypass insulation.
cards.explain: Examples include slab edges, steel studs and balcony connections; they can significantly reduce effective wall R-value.
wrong: A device that moves heat between two buildings
A layer that blocks moisture migration
An air gap behind rainscreen cladding

cards.q: What does SHGC measure?
cards.a: Fraction of incident solar radiation admitted through a window as heat.
cards.explain: Ranges 0 to 1; lower SHGC means less solar heat gain, useful on sunny facades in cooling-dominated spaces.
wrong: The window's U-value under summer conditions
Air leakage rate through the window frame

cards.q: What is spatial daylight autonomy (sDA)?
cards.a: Percent of floor area meeting a target illuminance for a share of occupied hours.
cards.explain: Commonly sDA300/50%: area getting at least 300 lux for at least 50% of occupied hours, from annual simulation.
wrong: Daylight factor measured on an overcast day
Hours per year with direct sun on a facade
Ratio of window area to floor area

cards.q: What does ASE (annual sunlight exposure) flag?
cards.a: Floor area receiving too much direct sunlight, indicating glare/overheating risk.
cards.explain: Typically area receiving over 1000 lux of direct sun for more than 250 occupied hours per year.
wrong: Hours when electric lighting is on

cards.q: What is window-to-wall ratio (WWR)?
cards.a: Glazed area divided by gross exterior wall area.
cards.explain: Higher WWR increases daylight potential but often raises heat loss, solar gain and glare; it is a key early design lever.
wrong: Window area divided by floor area
Opaque wall U-value over window U-value

cards.q: What does a heat pump COP of 3 mean?
cards.a: It delivers 3 units of heat per 1 unit of electricity.
cards.explain: COP is useful output over input energy; heat pumps exceed 1 because they move heat rather than generate it.
wrong: It is 3% more efficient than a furnace
It operates at 3 kW of capacity
It needs 3 units of electricity per unit of heat

cards.q: What is a DOAS?
cards.a: A dedicated outdoor air system that handles ventilation air separately.
cards.explain: DOAS decouples ventilation from heating and cooling, often paired with radiant panels, fan coils or VRF for space loads.
wrong: A rooftop unit with no outdoor air

cards.q: Main difference between VAV and radiant systems?
cards.a: VAV moves heat with air; radiant uses water through surfaces.
cards.explain: Radiant systems condition via surfaces and need separate ventilation (often DOAS); water carries heat more efficiently than air.
wrong: VAV only heats, radiant only cools
Radiant systems require more fan energy
VAV uses refrigerant, radiant uses steam

cards.q: ERV vs HRV: what's the difference?
cards.a: An ERV transfers heat and moisture; an HRV transfers heat only.
cards.explain: Both recover energy from exhaust air to precondition incoming ventilation air.
wrong: An HRV transfers moisture, an ERV does not
They are different names for an economizer
An ERV heats air with electric resistance

cards.q: Why size mechanical plant to design-day loads rather than averages?
cards.a: Plant must meet peak conditions, not typical ones.
cards.explain: Design days represent near-extreme conditions; sizing to averages would leave spaces uncomfortable at peak, while oversizing wastes cost and efficiency.
wrong: Average loads are always higher than peaks
Design days only matter for lighting

cards.q: What is EUI?
cards.a: Energy use intensity: annual energy use per unit floor area.
cards.explain: In the US typically kBtu/sf/yr; used to benchmark and compare buildings of different sizes.
wrong: Energy use per occupant per day
Efficiency rating of a single appliance

cards.q: Peak demand vs annual energy: what's the difference?
cards.a: Peak is maximum power (kW); annual is total energy over a year (kWh).
cards.explain: Peak drives equipment and grid sizing and demand charges; annual energy drives consumption costs and much of carbon.
wrong: They are the same metric in different units
Peak is measured in kWh, annual in kW

cards.q: Roughly how many kBtu are in one kWh?
cards.a: About 3.412 kBtu.
cards.explain: Useful for converting electric use into kBtu to compute EUI alongside gas use in therms.

cards.q: What is California's Title 24, Part 6?
cards.a: California's building energy efficiency standards.
cards.explain: Updated on a regular cycle by the California Energy Commission; recent cycles have increasingly favored heat pumps and electrification.

cards.q: What do local all-electric building ordinances generally do?
cards.a: Restrict or prohibit new natural gas infrastructure in new construction.
cards.explain: Several Bay Area jurisdictions, including San Francisco, adopted all-electric requirements for new buildings; details and legal status vary by jurisdiction.
wrong: Mandate gas backup for heat pumps

cards.q: Operational vs embodied carbon?
cards.a: Operational is from running the building; embodied is from materials and construction.
cards.explain: Embodied includes extraction, manufacturing, transport, construction, maintenance and end of life; operational comes mainly from energy use.
wrong: They are two names for the same thing

cards.q: Which EN 15978 modules are the 'product stage'?
cards.a: A1-A3: raw material supply, transport, and manufacturing.
cards.explain: A1-A3 is often called cradle-to-gate and is the scope most EPDs always report.

cards.q: What does EN 15978 module B6 cover?
cards.a: Operational energy use during the building's life.
cards.explain: B-stage modules cover the use stage; B7 is operational water use.

cards.q: What do C1-C4 and Module D represent?
cards.a: C is end-of-life; D is benefits and loads beyond the system boundary.
cards.explain: Module D captures potential reuse, recycling or energy recovery benefits and is reported separately.
wrong: C is construction, D is design
C is carbon offsets, D is daylight
C is commissioning, D is decommissioning

cards.q: What is an EPD?
cards.a: An Environmental Product Declaration: verified LCA results for a product.
cards.explain: Prepared to product category rules and third-party verified; product-specific EPDs are more precise than industry averages.
wrong: An energy performance disclosure for buildings

cards.q: What is EC3 used for?
cards.a: Comparing embodied carbon of materials using an EPD database.
cards.explain: EC3 by Building Transparency is a free tool popular for setting and comparing material GWP limits, e.g. concrete mixes.

cards.q: Name two whole-building LCA tools from the posting.
cards.a: Tally and One Click LCA (also Athena Impact Estimator).
cards.explain: Tally works inside Revit; One Click LCA is a web platform; Athena Impact Estimator is a free North American tool.

cards.q: What is simple payback?
cards.a: Upfront cost divided by annual savings, in years.
cards.explain: Easy to communicate but ignores time value of money and savings beyond the payback period.
wrong: Present value of all future savings
Annual savings divided by upfront cost times 100

cards.q: What does NPV capture that simple payback ignores?
cards.a: Time value of money across the whole analysis period.
cards.explain: NPV discounts future costs and savings to today; positive NPV means the investment beats the discount rate.

cards.q: Effect of a higher discount rate on long-term savings' present value?
cards.a: It reduces their present value.
cards.explain: Higher discount rates weight near-term cash flows more, making long-lived measures look less attractive.

cards.q: What is a building water balance?
cards.a: Comparison of water demand to supplies, including reuse and rainwater.
cards.explain: Used to size tanks and estimate how much potable water non-potable sources can offset.

cards.q: What are distributed energy resources (DERs)?
cards.a: Small, local generation, storage or flexible loads connected near use.
cards.explain: Examples: rooftop PV, batteries, EV chargers, controllable HVAC; they can serve buildings and support the grid.

cards.q: What does GEB stand for, per DOE?
cards.a: Grid-interactive efficient building.
cards.explain: Combines efficiency with smart controls and DERs to provide demand flexibility.

cards.q: What are DOE's demand flexibility modes?
cards.a: Shed, shift, modulate, and generate.
cards.explain: Buildings reduce load, move it in time, adjust it quickly for grid services, or produce power on site.

cards.q: What is passive survivability?
cards.a: Keeping a building habitable without power or fuel during disruptions.
cards.explain: Achieved through envelope performance, shading, natural ventilation and thermal mass so occupants can shelter in place.

cards.q: Name four LEED credit categories.
cards.a: Energy and Atmosphere, Water Efficiency, Materials and Resources, Indoor Environmental Quality.
cards.explain: Others include Location and Transportation, Sustainable Sites, Integrative Process, Innovation, Regional Priority.
wrong: Quality of Life, Leadership, Natural World, Climate

cards.q: Who administers LEED certification and credentials?
cards.a: USGBC develops LEED; GBCI handles certification and credentials.
cards.explain: Green Business Certification Inc. (GBCI) administers LEED project certification and professional exams.

cards.q: What is WELL primarily focused on?
cards.a: Human health and wellbeing in buildings.
cards.explain: WELL v2 organizes features into concepts like Air, Water, Light, Thermal Comfort, Sound and Mind, with performance verification.

cards.q: What is Fitwel?
cards.a: A health-focused building certification created by CDC and GSA.
cards.explain: Now operated by the Center for Active Design; known for evidence-based, relatively accessible strategies.

cards.q: What are Living Building Challenge 'petals'?
cards.a: Performance areas: Place, Water, Energy, Health and Happiness, Materials, Equity, Beauty.
cards.explain: LBC by ILFI requires demonstrated performance over a period of occupancy, not just design intent.

cards.q: What is Envision designed for?
cards.a: Rating sustainability of infrastructure projects.
cards.explain: Run by the Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure; categories include Quality of Life, Leadership, Resource Allocation, Natural World, Climate and Resilience.

cards.q: Who founded Arup?
cards.a: Sir Ove Arup, an engineer and philosopher.
cards.explain: He founded the firm in London in 1946; his 1970 'Key Speech' still frames the firm's values.

cards.q: How is Arup owned?
cards.a: Held in trust on behalf of its members (employees).
cards.explain: There are no external shareholders; members share in profits, supporting long-term, independent decisions.

cards.q: What global framework does Arup align its work with?
cards.a: The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
cards.explain: Arup aligns its strategy and project work with the 17 SDGs, e.g. clean energy, sustainable cities and climate action.

europe.title: Working in Madrid & Paris
points: The usual route: join the US office, build 2-3 years of experience, then ask for an internal transfer or a mobility assignment. Big firms with offices in all five cities make this possible.
You'll need the right to work in the EU (a work visa sponsored by the firm, an internal transfer, or EU citizenship). Ask about mobility programs in interviews.
Language: aim for B2-level Spanish or French. Client meetings and site work there happen in the local language.
Learn the European frameworks: BREEAM (more common in Europe than LEED), the EU Taxonomy and CSRD sustainability reporting, and the EU buildings directive (EPBD).
France: RE2020, the environmental regulation for new buildings, limits both energy use and lifecycle (embodied) carbon. It's a great talking point for embodied-carbon work.
Spain: the Codigo Tecnico de la Edificacion (CTE) sets energy and building requirements. Know that it exists and what its energy section covers.
